prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of the incretin hormone GLP-1 and its active form that made possible incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: one part, B003, with Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. The scientific case is a discovery arc and not a product story. Holst established the secretion and actions of GLP-1, Mojsov the identity and synthesis of the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide, and Drucker the receptor-level and proglucagon-derived peptide biology together with the therapeutic concept. Each step rests on specific experiments that were independently replicated. The result changed how type 2 diabetes and obesity are understood and treated, and the clinical effect is confirmed in large outcome trials including cardiovascular and renal endpoints. Maturity is not in question. The citation is deliberately worded around physiology and the active form of the hormone, so it does not claim that any one group alone identified the peptide, which is the way I would answer the chair's question on the Habener-group priority issue. I do not treat the unanimity of round 1 as evidence. All six of us read the same file, and I have weighed the case on its content.
statement.case_against: Attribution remains the weak point and round 1 did not resolve it. Mojsov's priority for the active peptide is contested, and the Habener group lies outside the credited names. I cannot settle that from the supplied material. Knudsen's medicinal chemistry produced the long-acting agonists that reached patients, so leaving her out can look arbitrary, and a discovery-anchored prize invites the question of why drug developers are excluded. The three-person cap makes some exclusion unavoidable. If the documented record showed that Mojsov's contribution was not decisive, the right response would be to reconsider her seat explicitly and not to widen the prize to drug development by default. Long-term safety of chronic incretin use is also still accruing, though I do not regard that as a maturity obstacle.

responses.point: The chair moved toward the discovery-anchored reading in round 1 and now supports Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, while noting that his opening ballot preferred Knudsen and that the third seat is open.
responses.response: I welcome the move and I answer his question on the third seat directly. I keep Mojsov because the active peptide is the discovery-stage step that made the downstream pharmacology possible, while lead optimisation of liraglutide and semaglutide is translation, and a prize that included it would raise the question of the other drug developers. I stay open on one condition. If someone shows from the documented record that Mojsov's role in the active form is overstated, I would revisit the seat and consider Knudsen. A contested claim alone does not meet that bar. On B043 he is right that disease relevance is still developing, and I cannot argue otherwise. I disclose our co-authorship again below.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius would not support B043 as a second part because disease relevance is asserted more than demonstrated and the PERK and ATF6 arms (Ron, Harding, Kaufman) are outside the credited names. She keeps B015 and B010 as alternatives.
responses.response: The point about the PERK and ATF6 arms is fair, and I accept that Walter and Mori describe the IRE1-HAC1/XBP1 discovery core and not the whole pathway. That is a statement about scope, and it is not an attribution defect, because the credited pair holds the original signalling discovery. I concede that a second part now would need us to accept a basic-science prize with human relevance still developing. Given the strength of B003, I no longer press for a second part this year, and I keep B043 as an alternative for a later year. On B010 I still read the imatinib work as translation of earlier BCR-ABL discoveries (Rowley, Baltimore and others outside the trio), so I do not move it above B043 or B015.

responses.point: Linnarsson agrees with the Holst, Drucker and Mojsov trio and my reading of Knudsen, but ranks B043 below CAR-T and SMN2 antisense because its link to human disease is still being worked out.
responses.response: I accept the weighting argument against B043 and I have adjusted. Placing it above CAR-T as a second part is not supportable for me when its clinical link is still developing. I keep it as a first alternative on conceptual grounds only. On B015 I share his and the Wahren-Herlenius concern about Eshhar. A citation could credit the clinical and engineering development of the therapy without implying that June, Sadelain and Rosenberg conceived the chimeric receptor, but I would need to see the wording and the pair question (June and Sadelain with or without Rosenberg) settled first. I also agree that the shortfall in B040 is follow-up time, not scientific quality.

responses.point: El-Manira keeps B036 (optogenetics) as an alternative and prefers a discovery-anchored B003, noting that the attribution weakness lies in the Mojsov versus Habener question and not in the science.
responses.response: I agree with him that a discovery-anchored prize is better supported than a drug-development one and that the problem is attribution, not merit. On B036 I still cannot find a defensible three-person subset of the six credited names. Channelrhodopsin discovery (Nagel, Hegemann, Bamberg) and neuronal deployment (Deisseroth, Boyden) are distinct contributions, and Miesenböck's earlier approach further complicates the question. I would not choose among them under the three-person cap, so I leave B036 outside my alternatives.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's contribution to the active GLP-1 peptide can be defended against the Habener group's work, which cannot be resolved from the supplied names.
Whether the third seat should go to Mojsov or Knudsen, which turns on whether the prize honours discovery alone or discovery plus drug development.

Whether a second part would strengthen the prize or dilute a case that already stands alone. B043 lacks demonstrated clinical consequence, and B015 needs a fair treatment of Eshhar and the Rosenberg question.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with any credited shortlisted candidate is apparent from my profile. My research on nuclear receptors and dopamine neurons does not overlap with B003, B043 or B015, and Ronald Evans, with whom I worked at Salk, is not credited on any shortlisted ballot. I have about twenty co-authored works with Per Svenningsson, the chair, and one with Abdel El Manira (2009). These are collegial ties and not ties to a candidate. I disclose them again for transparency. Neither of them changes my assessment.
